The earlier pages of this track turned Larkspur Re's year event loss table into
annual ceded losses. This page turns one contract's ceded losses into a price.
The story, the files and the notation are on [the overview](cat-0-overview.qmd).
The contract is `alder_cat_1`, Larkspur's 30% line on Alder Mutual's first cat
layer, 40 xs 30 with one reinstatement at 100%. Its terms come from
`examples/data/cat_book_contracts.csv`, as on every page.

This is the R twin of the Python guide [`cat-6-pricing.md`](cat-6-pricing.md):
the same sections, the same files and the same numbers. Each R chunk is followed
by the text it prints, and `R/prospicio/tests/test-guides.R` requires each one
to print exactly that text, the same text as the Python guide's.

A price has three parts. The expected loss pays the claims on average. A risk
load, the margin above the expected loss
([risk loads and distortions](risk-loads-and-distortions.md)), pays for the
capital that stands behind the bad years. Expenses and brokerage come on top. The sections below build each part, then ask what the
reinstatement premium does to the price, how sensitive the answer is, and
whether the market's rate on line is enough.

## 1. The contract's ceded losses

The helper `cedent_events()` is the same on every page of the track: it reads
the YELT for one cedent and keeps each loss's time in the year and its peril.
The tests run the guides from the repository root and Quarto renders them from
`docs/guides/`, so `find_data()` looks for `examples/data/` upwards from the
working directory. The layer is built from the contract's row. Larkspur's
upfront premium is the rate on line times the limit times its share.

```{r}
library(prospicio)

# The data files, found from the repository root (CI) or from docs/guides (Quarto).
find_data <- function(name, dir = getwd()) {
  repeat {
    path <- file.path(dir, "examples", "data", name)
    if (file.exists(path)) return(path)
    parent <- dirname(dir)
    if (identical(parent, dir)) stop("examples/data/", name, " not found", call. = FALSE)
    dir <- parent
  }
}
read_book <- function(name) {
  utils::read.csv(find_data(name), colClasses = "character", na.strings = character())
}

YELT <- utils::read.csv(find_data("cat_book_yelt.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
CONTRACTS <- split(read_book("cat_book_contracts.csv"), ~contract)
N_YEARS <- 2000
cedent_events <- function(cedent, perils = "all") {
  rows <- YELT[YELT$cedent == cedent, ]
  if (perils != "all") rows <- rows[rows$peril %in% strsplit(perils, "+", fixed = TRUE)[[1]], ]
  year <- factor(rows$year, levels = seq_len(N_YEARS))
  time <- ((rows$day - 1) * 24 + rows$hour) / 8760
  ev <- events_from_years(unname(split(rows$loss, year)), times = unname(split(time, year)))
  with_labels(ev, list(peril = unlist(split(rows$peril, year), use.names = FALSE)))
}

# An occurrence excess of loss layer from a row of the contracts file.
xl_layer <- function(c, pro_rata_time = FALSE) {
  limit <- as.numeric(c$limit); share <- as.numeric(c$share)
  xol_layer(c$contract, limit, as.numeric(c$attachment), share = share,
            premium = as.numeric(c$rate_on_line) * limit * share,
            reinstatement_rates = rep(as.numeric(c$reinstatement_rate), as.integer(c$reinstatements)),
            pro_rata_time = pro_rata_time)
}

# The layer's annual ceded loss and reinstatement premium, one draw a year.
ceded_and_rip <- function(layer, events) {
  res <- aggregate(apply_tower(reinsurance_tower(list(layer)), events), keep = c("kind", "layer"))
  list(loss = marginal(res, list(kind = "ceded", layer = layer@name)),
       rip = marginal(res, list(kind = "reinstatement_premium", layer = layer@name)))
}

c1 <- CONTRACTS[["alder_cat_1"]]
raw <- cedent_events("alder")
grouped <- hours_clause(raw, as.numeric(c1$hours))
lay <- xl_layer(c1)
cr <- ceded_and_rip(lay, grouped)
loss <- cr$loss; rip <- cr$rip
X <- sampled(loss@draws)
cat(sprintf("limit at Larkspur's share %.1f, upfront premium %.4f\n", lay@limit * lay@share, lay@premium))
cat(sprintf("expected ceded loss %.4f, loss ratio %.3f\n", mean(X), mean(X) / lay@premium))
cat(sprintf("years with a ceded loss %d of %d\n", sum(loss@draws > 0), N_YEARS))
```

```text
limit at Larkspur's share 12.0, upfront premium 1.8000
expected ceded loss 0.8230, loss ratio 0.457
years with a ceded loss 230 of 2000
```

The loss ratio matches the table in page 3, section 6. Most years cost the layer nothing,
and a few cost it the whole line. That shape is why the risk load matters more
than the expected loss for a cat layer.

## 2. Cost of capital

Larkspur holds assets `A` against the layer's bad years, of which the premium
`P` is part and capital `K = A - P` the rest
([a first course](a-first-course.qmd) and
[what a reinsurance price is](reinsurance-price.md), a Python guide, explain
the idea). With a cost of capital `r`, the margin `P - EL` must equal `r K`.
Solve for `P`:

```
P = (EL + r A) / (1 + r),    K = A - P
```

Here the assets are the TVaR at 99% of the ceded loss: the mean of the worst 1%
of years. Note the convention. A common shortcut is `EL + r (TVaR - EL)`, which
charges for capital as if the premium did not help pay the tail. prospicio's
`risk_loaded_price()` counts the premium as part of the assets, so the capital
and the price are both a little lower.

```{r}
p <- risk_loaded_price(X, distortion("tvar", 0.99), cost_of_capital = 0.10)
cat(sprintf("expected loss %.4f\n", p$expected_loss))
cat(sprintf("assets (TVaR 99) %.4f\n", p$assets))
cat(sprintf("premium %.4f, capital %.4f\n", p$premium, p$capital))
cat(sprintf("margin %.4f, return on capital %.4f\n", p$margin, p$return_on_capital))
cat(sprintf("by the formula %.4f\n", (p$expected_loss + 0.10 * p$assets) / 1.10))
cat(sprintf("shortcut EL + r (TVaR - EL) %.4f\n", p$expected_loss + 0.10 * (p$assets - p$expected_loss)))
```

```text
expected loss 0.8230
assets (TVaR 99) 13.8428
premium 2.0066, capital 11.8362
margin 1.1836, return on capital 0.1000
by the formula 2.0066
shortcut EL + r (TVaR - EL) 2.1250
```

## 3. A distortion price

A pricing distortion reweights the years, heavier in the tail, and the premium
is the expected loss under the new weights; the return on the same capital
then falls out of the price.
[Risk loads and distortions](risk-loads-and-distortions.md) compares the
families and [portfolio pricing](pir-portfolio-pricing.qmd) the theory. Here
the Wang transform with a parameter of 0.3.

```{r}
pw <- risk_loaded_price(X, distortion("tvar", 0.99), distortion = distortion("wang", 0.3))
cat(sprintf("Wang 0.3 premium %.4f, capital %.4f\n", pw$premium, pw$capital))
cat(sprintf("return on capital %.4f\n", pw$return_on_capital))
```

```text
Wang 0.3 premium 1.4225, capital 12.4204
return on capital 0.0483
```

The Wang price is lower, and the return it implies on the TVaR capital is under
5%. The two rules answer different questions. Choose the one your capital
model is calibrated to, and read the other as a check.

## 4. From risk premium to a quote

The premium above is the risk premium. With expenses `e` and brokerage `b` as
fractions of the quoted premium `Q`, `Q = P / (1 - e - b)`
([what a reinsurance price is](reinsurance-price.md), "The technical
premium"). `technical_quote()` does this and reports the rate on line against the limit at
Larkspur's share.

```{r}
q <- technical_quote(p, expenses = 0.05, brokerage = 0.10, limit = lay@limit * lay@share)
cat(sprintf("technical premium %.4f, rate on line %.4f\n", q$premium, q$rate_on_line))
cat(sprintf("expenses %.4f, brokerage %.4f, risk premium %.4f\n", q$expenses, q$brokerage, q$risk_premium))
cat(sprintf("contract rate on line %.2f, premium %.4f\n", as.numeric(c1$rate_on_line), lay@premium))
```

```text
technical premium 2.3607, rate on line 0.1967
expenses 0.1180, brokerage 0.2361, risk premium 2.0066
contract rate on line 0.15, premium 1.8000
```

The technical rate on line is above the 15% in the contract. Section 7 asks
what the contract's price earns.

## 5. The reinstatement premium inside the price

When the layer pays a loss, the cedent buys the limit back. With one
reinstatement at 100%, the cedent pays the upfront premium again in proportion
to the limit used. So the reinsurer collects more than the upfront premium in
exactly the years it pays claims.

**Expected value.** Each year's reinstatement premium is the upfront premium
times a factor that depends only on the losses: the share of the limit used,
times the rate. So its expected value is `f P` for a fixed `f`. If the risk
premium `R` must come from the upfront premium and the expected reinstatement
premium together, then `P (1 + f) = R`, and `P = R / (1 + f)` in closed form.

```{r}
f <- mean(rip) / lay@premium
cat(sprintf("expected reinstatement premium %.4f, f = %.5f\n", mean(rip), f))
cat(sprintf("upfront premium for a risk premium of %.4f: %.4f\n", p$premium, p$premium / (1 + f)))
```

```text
expected reinstatement premium 0.1207, f = 0.06705
upfront premium for a risk premium of 2.0066: 1.8805
```

**In the tail.** Under TVaR the expected value is not the whole story. Each
year's reinstatement premium is `P g_t`, where `g_t` depends only on that
year's losses, and it arrives in the years with losses, so it also lowers the
tail of the net outcome `X_t - P g_t`. The assets then depend on `P`, and the
upfront premium solves `P = price(X - P g)`, one equation in one unknown.
Sundt (1991) and Mata (2000) study premiums with reinstatements in this
spirit. prospicio has no call for it (#587), so the chunk below
finds the root by bisection: the price of the net outcome falls as `P`
rises, so `price(X - P g) - P` changes sign once between 0 and the price
without reinstatement premium.

```{r}
g <- rip@draws / lay@premium  # reinstatement premium per unit of upfront premium
gap <- function(P) {
  risk_loaded_price(sampled(loss@draws - P * g), distortion("tvar", 0.99), cost_of_capital = 0.10)$premium - P
}
lo <- 0
hi <- p$premium
while (hi - lo > 1e-10) {
  mid <- (lo + hi) / 2
  if (gap(mid) > 0) lo <- mid else hi <- mid
}
P <- (lo + hi) / 2
p_net <- risk_loaded_price(sampled(loss@draws - P * g), distortion("tvar", 0.99), cost_of_capital = 0.10)
cat(sprintf("upfront premium %.4f, assets of the net outcome %.4f\n", P, p_net$assets))
cat(sprintf("quoted with 5%% expenses and 10%% brokerage %.4f\n", P / (1 - 0.05 - 0.10)))
```

```text
upfront premium 1.7421, assets of the net outcome 12.1008
quoted with 5% expenses and 10% brokerage 2.0495
```

Counting the reinstatement premium in the tail lowers the upfront premium
further than the expected value alone does. The gap is the capital the
reinstatement premium saves in the worst years.

## 6. Sensitivity

A price is only as firm as its inputs. Three are worth a loop: the cost of
capital, the hours clause and the timing of the season.

**Cost of capital.** The assets do not change with `r`, but the premium is
concave in it: `P = (EL + r A) / (1 + r)` rises by less with each step.

```{r}
for (r in c(0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20)) {
  cat(sprintf("r = %.2f: premium %.4f\n", r,
              risk_loaded_price(X, distortion("tvar", 0.99), cost_of_capital = r)$premium))
}
```

```text
r = 0.05: premium 1.4430
r = 0.10: premium 2.0066
r = 0.15: premium 2.5212
r = 0.20: premium 2.9930
```

**Hours clause.** Without the 72 hour clause, the pieces of a split windstorm
or convective storm are separate occurrences, each with its own retention.

```{r}
loss_raw <- ceded_and_rip(lay, raw)$loss
for (case in list(list("72 hours", loss), list("no clause", loss_raw))) {
  pr <- risk_loaded_price(sampled(case[[2]]@draws), distortion("tvar", 0.99), cost_of_capital = 0.10)
  cat(sprintf("%9s: expected loss %.4f, assets %.4f, premium %.4f\n", case[[1]],
              pr$expected_loss, pr$assets, pr$premium))
}
```

```text
 72 hours: expected loss 0.8230, assets 13.8428, premium 2.0066
no clause: expected loss 0.7778, assets 15.4227, premium 2.1092
```

The clause raises the expected loss, since the pieces of a storm add up before
the retention applies. It lowers the tail. Without it, a storm that arrives in
two large pieces can take the full limit twice in one year, once from the
limit and once from the reinstatement. Grouped, the same storm is one
occurrence and takes one limit. On this book the tail effect wins, and the
price without the clause is higher.

**Season.** A reinstatement pro rata as to time charges only for the part of
the year left. Most of Alder's windstorms (nine in ten in the generator)
arrive between day 213 and day 305, so the cedent pays much less to
reinstate, and `f` falls.

```{r}
rip_time <- ceded_and_rip(xl_layer(c1, pro_rata_time = TRUE), grouped)$rip
f_time <- mean(rip_time) / lay@premium
cat(sprintf("f pro rata as to amount %.5f, as to time %.5f\n", f, f_time))
cat(sprintf("upfront premium (expected value) %.4f against %.4f\n", p$premium / (1 + f), p$premium / (1 + f_time)))
```

```text
f pro rata as to amount 0.06705, as to time 0.02484
upfront premium (expected value) 1.8805 against 1.9580
```

## 7. Is the market price adequate?

The contract's rate on line is 15%, a premium of 1.8 at Larkspur's share.
`implied_quote()` reads a quoted premium backwards: it takes off expenses and
brokerage, and reports the margin and the return on the same capital.

```{r}
m <- implied_quote(q, lay@premium)
cat(sprintf("quoted premium %.4f, risk premium %.4f\n", m$premium, m$risk_premium))
cat(sprintf("loss ratio %.3f, margin %.4f\n", m$loss_ratio, m$margin))
cat(sprintf("return on capital %.4f against a target of 0.10\n", m$return_on_capital))
```

```text
quoted premium 1.8000, risk premium 1.5300
loss ratio 0.457, margin 0.7070
return on capital 0.0574 against a target of 0.10
```

At the market's price, `alder_cat_1` earns well under the 10% target on its
stand-alone capital. The reinstatement premium does not close the gap: with
it counted in the tail, section 5's upfront premium of 1.7421 is a risk
premium, and grossed up for expenses and brokerage it is 2.0495, still above
the 1.8 charged. What is left is diversification in Larkspur's book, which
page 7 measures. prospicio has no single report that sets the price, the
return and the target side by side for a deal (#589).

## What is missing

- an upfront premium that counts the reinstatement premium in the price, in
  one call (#587)
- a report of a deal's price adequacy and return on capital (#589)
